title: Doudna & Charpentier: The Molecular Scissors of CRISPR
source_book: A Programmable Dual-RNA-Guided DNA Endonuclease in Adaptive Bacterial Immunity (Science, Vol. 337)
source_author: Martin Jinek, Krzysztof Chylinski, Ines Fonfara, Michael Hauer, Jennifer A. Doudna, Emmanuelle Charpentier
source_edition: American Association for the Advancement of Science
authenticity_note: Based on Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier's breakthrough 2012 paper repurposing bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 as a programmable genome-editing technology, winning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
summary: Investigating how humble bacteria defend themselves against attacking viruses, biochemists Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier teamed up in 2011. They reprogrammed an ancient bacterial enzyme called Cas9 with a synthetic guide RNA, inventing precision molecular scissors that can edit the DNA of any living organism like correcting a typo in a word processor.
content:
For billions of years, an invisible war has raged across every puddle of water, drop of soil, and inside our own guts: the war between bacteria and the ravenous viruses that prey on them, known as bacteriophages.

In the late 2000s, microbiologists discovered something strange inside bacterial genomes: mysterious, repeating sequences dubbed **CRISPR** (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats). Tucked between the repeating palindromes were snippets of DNA stolen from past viral invaders! Bacteria were keeping a biological mugshot gallery of their enemies.

In March 2011, at a microbiology conference in San Juan, Puerto Rico, American biochemist Jennifer Doudna met French microbiologist Emmanuelle Charpentier. Over coffee and a stroll through the cobblestone streets of Old San Juan, they realized their complementary strengths: Charpentier had uncovered how a molecule called *tracrRNA* paired with CRISPR, while Doudna was a world expert on the structural biochemistry of RNA enzymes.

They decided to join forces across the Atlantic.

In their laboratories at UC Berkeley and Umeå University, they focused on an enzyme called **Cas9**—the executioner protein. Working through brilliant biochemical assays, their teams demonstrated that Cas9 acted like a molecular sentinel: armed with a matching RNA guide, it roamed the cell, locked onto invading viral DNA matching the guide, and cleanly sliced both strands in two like microscopic scissors!

Then came the flash of pure genius: Doudna and Charpentier engineered a single synthetic **Guide RNA** that fused the two natural RNA components. By simply typing any custom genetic sequence into their guide RNA, they could command Cas9 to cut *any* gene, in *any* cell—from plants and animals to human beings—at a precise letter!

Published in *Science* in August 2012, this breakthrough transformed biology overnight. Scientists could now rewrite the code of life with the precision of a word processor, opening doors to curing sickle cell anemia, genetic blindness, and muscular dystrophy. In 2020, Doudna and Charpentier were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry—the first all-female scientific duo to win the honor.

stem_vocabulary.definition: A revolutionary gene-editing technology adapted from a bacterial defense mechanism that precisely cuts targeted DNA sequences.
A synthetic RNA molecule that guides the Cas9 enzyme to a specific matching sequence in the genome.
An enzyme that cleaves a polynucleotide chain by separating nucleotides other than the two end ones.
A type of genetic engineering in which DNA is inserted, deleted, modified, or replaced in the genome of a living organism.
